title: Making peace
hook: Aaron's way, lived: help two people reconcile
tomorrow: exiles in an enemy city get a letter. what does it tell them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, tochachah: a concern raised privately, gently, so it can be heard. Rebuke with love. Today, when the fight isn't yours, but you're standing in the middle of it.

Two people at one lunch table who won't look at each other. You can hear it: forks a little too loud, a silence where the jokes used to be. You're friends with both. A collection of teachings called Avot de-Rabbi Natan says Aaron, the brother of Moses, had a way into exactly that silence. When two people quarreled, he went to each one alone. And what he said to each was the same.
screen: `FORKS A LITTLE TOO LOUD.` → `FRIENDS WITH BOTH.` → `AARON WENT TO EACH ALONE.`

segments.voice: He'd sit with the first and say: look at your friend. He's tearing at his heart, saying, how can I face him? I'm ashamed. I'm the one who wronged him. Aaron would sit there until the anger left that heart. Then he'd go to the other and say the same. And when the two met, the text says, they embraced and kissed. Hillel turns this into a calling in Pirkei Avot: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Pursuing. Peace doesn't wait to be found; somebody chases it. Did the other one really say those words? The text doesn't tell us. But here's the line to tell a friend tonight. The Talmud says it's allowed to change a detail for the sake of peace, and it points to God doing it. When Sarah laughed that her husband was too old, God told Abraham only that Sarah had called herself old. Aaron's way isn't lying about what matters. It's carrying the softest true thing across the room, and going first. The embrace belongs to them. The walking back and forth belongs to whoever pursues peace.
screen: `HE'S ASHAMED. HE WANTS YOU BACK.` · `THEN THE SAME TO THE OTHER.` · `LOVING PEACE, PURSUING PEACE.` · `A DETAIL CHANGED FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `PURSUE PEACE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, one for each person in a quarrel you know. With each slow breath, lift them a little closer, until the palms meet. Hold them there, and think of one true, kind thing each of them might want the other to hear.
screen: `ONE HAND FOR EACH.` · `CLOSER WITH EACH BREATH.` · `ONE TRUE, KIND THING.`

segments.voice: Making peace: Aaron's way, going to each side alone with the softest true thing, until two people can meet.
Something to keep: pursue peace. Somebody has to walk back and forth for it. Day done.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching holds up Aaron as the model peacemaker; Pirkei Avot calls people to be his disciples, loving and pursuing peace, and the tradition allows small changes of detail for the sake of peace between people.

Avot de-Rabbi Natan.meaning: an early companion to Pirkei Avot, full of stories

Aaron.meaning: the brother of Moses, a priest and peacemaker

Hillel.meaning: an early sage who taught love of peace

Pirkei Avot.meaning: a book of the Mishnah: sayings of the sages

sources.ref: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 12 (Aaron goes to each of two who quarreled, says the other is ashamed and wants peace; they embrace when they meet)
Mishnah Avot 1:12 (Hillel: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace)
Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b (it is permitted to alter a detail for the sake of peace; God reported Sarah's words without 'my lord being old')
Genesis 18:12-13 (Sarah laughs; God tells Abraham she said she was old)
